- [React development environment](https://www.palantir.com/docs/foundry/ontology-sdk-react-applications/development)

Vite is the default bundler for apps created with `@osdk/create-app`. This page covers the Vite settings an OSDK app needs and why.

> [!NOTE]
> The React template in `@osdk/create-app` already includes these settings in its generated `vite.config.ts`. Read on if you add OSDK to an existing Vite app or want to know what the generated config does.

## Define `process.env.NODE_ENV`

OSDK packages read `process.env.NODE_ENV` to decide how much to log and to strip development-only code from production builds. Vite does not replace `process.env` by default, so the browser throws:

```txt
ReferenceError: process is not defined
```

Tell Vite to replace `process.env.NODE_ENV` with the current mode:

```ts title="vite.config.ts"
import react from "@vitejs/plugin-react";
import { defineConfig } from "vite";

export default defineConfig(({ mode }) => {
  return {
    plugins: [react()],
    define: {
      "process.env.NODE_ENV": JSON.stringify(mode),
    },
  };
});
```

`vite dev` runs in `development` mode and `vite build` in `production` mode, so production bundles get `"production"`.

## Proxy Foundry requests in development

The browser blocks requests from `http://localhost:8080` to your Foundry stack unless the stack allows that origin for CORS. If you cannot get localhost allowed, proxy the requests through the Vite dev server instead. `@osdk/create-app` generates this setup when you answer yes to the CORS proxy prompt or pass `--corsProxy true`:

### Proxy the API paths

Forward `/api` and `/multipass/api` to your Foundry URL:

```ts title="vite.config.ts"
import react from "@vitejs/plugin-react";
import { defineConfig } from "vite";

export default defineConfig(({ mode }) => {
  return {
    plugins: [react()],
    server: {
      port: 8080,
      proxy: {
        "^(/multipass/api|/api)": {
          target: "https://your-stack.palantirfoundry.com",
          changeOrigin: true,
          secure: true,
        },
      },
    },
    define: {
      "process.env.NODE_ENV": JSON.stringify(mode),
    },
  };
});
```
### Point the client at the dev server

Set the Foundry URL that the client uses to the dev server's origin, so requests go through the proxy:

```sh title=".env.development"
VITE_FOUNDRY_API_URL=http://localhost:8080
VITE_FOUNDRY_REDIRECT_URL=http://localhost:8080/auth/callback
```

Pass that URL to both `createPublicOauthClient` and `createClient`. The OAuth calls under `/multipass/api` and the data calls under `/api` then reach Foundry through the proxy.
### Allow the redirect URL

Add `http://localhost:8080/auth/callback` as a redirect URL on the OAuth client in Developer Console.

The proxy runs only under `vite dev`. Production builds call Foundry directly, so keep the real Foundry URL in `.env.production`. Once your stack allows `http://localhost:8080` for CORS, you can remove the proxy and set `VITE_FOUNDRY_API_URL` back to the Foundry URL.

## Add OSDK Devtools

`@osdk/react-devtools` ships a Vite plugin that injects an inspection panel into your app during `vite dev` and does nothing in production builds:

```ts title="vite.config.ts"
import { osdkDevTools } from "@osdk/react-devtools/vite";
import react from "@vitejs/plugin-react";
import { defineConfig } from "vite";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react(), osdkDevTools()],
});
```

See [OSDK Devtools](https://older.zaini.me/osdk-ts/devtools.md) for installation, options, and the panel tabs.

# Installation

Source: https://older.zaini.me/osdk-ts/installation

> Add @osdk/client, @osdk/oauth, @osdk/react, and your generated SDK to an existing app, with the npm registry setup and version rules they need.

Related Palantir Foundry documentation:
- [Add OSDK to an existing app](https://www.palantir.com/docs/foundry/developer-console/how-to-add-to-existing-typescript)

Add OSDK to an app you already have by installing the client packages and your generated SDK from your Foundry npm registry. To start from a new project with everything configured, use the [Quickstart](https://older.zaini.me/osdk-ts/quickstart.md) instead.

## Before you start

Generate an SDK for your application in Developer Console with the **npm** package type, and note three values from its install instructions:

| Value | Example |
| --- | --- |
| SDK package name | `@my-app/sdk` |
| npm registry URL | `https://example.palantirfoundry.com/artifacts/api/repositories/ri.artifacts.main.repository.<id>/contents/release/npm` |
| Foundry token | A token that can read that registry. Keep it out of source control. |

## Install

### Point your SDK's scope at the Foundry registry

The generated SDK is not on the public npm registry. Add two lines to `.npmrc` in your project root: one maps your SDK's scope to the Foundry registry, and one authenticates every request to Foundry's artifacts API with a token from the environment.

```ini title=".npmrc"
//example.palantirfoundry.com/artifacts/api/:_authToken=${FOUNDRY_TOKEN}
@my-app:registry=https://example.palantirfoundry.com/artifacts/api/repositories/ri.artifacts.main.repository.<id>/contents/release/npm/
```

Replace `example.palantirfoundry.com` with your Foundry host, `@my-app` with your SDK's scope, and the registry URL with yours. Keep the trailing `/` on the registry URL, which pnpm requires. This is the same file `@osdk/create-app` writes.

Export the token before you install, and set it as a secret in CI:

```sh
export FOUNDRY_TOKEN=<token>
```
### Install the client packages and your SDK

```npm
npm install @osdk/client @osdk/api @osdk/oauth @my-app/sdk@latest
```

| Package | Why you need it |
| --- | --- |
| `@osdk/client` | `createClient` and the runtime that runs queries and actions. |
| `@osdk/api` | Types shared by the client and your SDK. |
| `@osdk/oauth` | Token providers for signing users in. See [Authentication](https://older.zaini.me/osdk-ts/authentication.md). |
| `@my-app/sdk` | Your Ontology's generated definitions. |
### Add the React packages

Skip this step if you do not use React.

```npm
npm install @osdk/react react react-dom
```

`@osdk/react` supports React 17, 18, and 19. For prebuilt components, also install `@osdk/react-components`; its setup is on [Components prerequisites](https://older.zaini.me/osdk-ts/components/prerequisites.md).
### Create the client

Create one client for your app and wrap your React tree in `OsdkProvider`. [Create a client](https://older.zaini.me/osdk-ts/client.md) walks through both.

## Version compatibility

`@osdk/client`, `@osdk/api`, and `@osdk/react` are released together and share a version number. `@osdk/react` imports its cache runtime from `@osdk/client/observable`, which is tied to the exact release line, so a mismatch fails at build time even when npm's peer ranges are satisfied.

- **Install the same version of all three.** If `@osdk/react` is `2.83.0`, use `@osdk/client@2.83.0` and `@osdk/api@2.83.0`.
- **Keep prereleases together.** A prerelease `@osdk/react`, such as `-beta.3`, needs the same prerelease of `@osdk/client` and `@osdk/api`. Pairing it with stable releases breaks.
- **Upgrade them in one command.** Bump the three packages together, and include `@osdk/react-components` if you use it:

  ```npm
  npm install @osdk/client@latest @osdk/api@latest @osdk/react@latest
  ```

- **Your generated SDK has a peer dependency on `@osdk/client`.** It is set to the client version that generated it, so install an `@osdk/client` that satisfies the SDK's peer range. When you upgrade the client across many versions, generate a new SDK version too.

A version mismatch usually shows up as one of these errors:

| Error | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `"<name>" is not exported by @osdk/client/.../observable.js` (or `@osdk/api/...`) | `@osdk/client` or `@osdk/api` is on a different release line than `@osdk/react`, often a prerelease paired with stable versions. | Install the exact `@osdk/client` and `@osdk/api` versions that match `@osdk/react`. |
| npm or pnpm peer warning for `@osdk/client` or `@osdk/api` | The declared peer ranges allow newer `@osdk/client` and `@osdk/api` releases than `@osdk/react` was built with, and, since `2.87.0`, warn on older ones. | Pin the matching versions instead of ignoring the warning. |

**Find matching versions for an older @osdk/react**

Before `2.15.0`, `@osdk/react` was versioned separately (`0.x`). To find the `@osdk/client` and `@osdk/api` versions it was built against:

1. Open `node_modules/@osdk/react/CHANGELOG.md`.
2. Find the heading for your installed `@osdk/react` version.
3. If that entry has an **Updated dependencies** section, install the exact `@osdk/client` and `@osdk/api` versions it lists.
4. If it does not, walk back to the closest earlier entry that does, and use those versions.

Upgrading to `2.15.0` or later is simpler: from then on the three versions match.
**npm cannot resolve peer dependencies**

If npm reports a peer conflict for OSDK packages after you have aligned versions, tell it to reuse your direct dependency versions with `overrides`:

```json title="package.json"
{
  "overrides": {
    "@osdk/client": "$@osdk/client",
    "@osdk/react": "$@osdk/react"
  }
}
```

## Optional peers for Platform APIs

Hooks from `@osdk/react/platform-apis`, such as `useCurrentFoundryUser`, `useFoundryUser`, and `useMarkings`, call Foundry Platform APIs through two optional peer dependencies. Install them only if you import from that entry point:

```npm
npm install @osdk/foundry.admin @osdk/foundry.core
```

Without them, a build that imports `@osdk/react/platform-apis` fails with `Rollup failed to resolve import "@osdk/foundry.admin"` (or `@osdk/foundry.core`). See [Platform APIs](https://older.zaini.me/osdk-ts/react/platform-apis.md).

## Bundler setup

OSDK packages read `process.env.NODE_ENV`, which Vite does not define by default. Without it the browser throws `ReferenceError: process is not defined`. [Use OSDK with Vite](https://older.zaini.me/osdk-ts/guides/vite.md) shows the `define` setting and a local CORS proxy to Foundry.

# Import existing types

Source: https://older.zaini.me/osdk-ts/ontology-as-code/import

> Convert an existing Foundry ontology's metadata into TypeScript with @osdk/maker-import, and reference those types from your ontology-as-code definitions.

{/* cspell:ignore geospatial */}

`@osdk/maker-import` turns the metadata of an ontology that already exists in Foundry into TypeScript modules. Import those modules into your `.ontology/ontology.mts` file to link to, implement, or reuse existing types without redefining them.

Imported types are references, not definitions: maker writes them to the IR's `importedOntology` section, and your ontology does not create or change them.

## Install

```npm
npm install --save-dev @osdk/maker-import @osdk/maker
```

## Get the ontology metadata

`maker-import` reads an `OntologyFullMetadata` JSON file, the response of the Foundry endpoint `GET /api/v2/ontologies/{ontology}/fullMetadata`. Two ways to get it:

- **From the OSDK CLI.** `osdk unstable typescript generate` with `--foundryUrl`, `--clientId`, and `--ontologyWritePath ontology-full-metadata.json` signs you in, fetches the metadata, and writes it to that path while it generates an SDK.
- **From the API.** Call the endpoint with a token that can read the ontology, and save the response.

## Generate the modules

```sh
npx maker-import -i ontology-full-metadata.json -o .ontology/imports
```

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-i`, `--input` | `string` | | Required. The `OntologyFullMetadata` JSON file. |
| `-o`, `--output` | `string` | `./generated-imports` | The output directory. |

The output has one module per type and an `index.ts` that re-exports them all:

```text
imports/
  index.ts
  codegen/
    shared-property-types/
    interface-types/
    object-types/
    action-types/
```

Each export is named after the type's API name, without its namespace, in camelCase: `Employee` becomes `employee` and `modify-employee` becomes `modifyEmployee`. When two types share a short name, both use the full API name instead, such as `comExampleEmployee`, and any remaining clash gets a numeric suffix. Each run deletes and rewrites the four `codegen` folders.

## Use imported types

Each export is a proxy. The first time your ontology reads one of its properties, maker records the type as imported, along with the shared property types its properties use. Exports you never touch stay out of the IR.

```ts title=".ontology/ontology.mts"
import { defineLink, defineObject } from "@osdk/maker";

import { employee } from "./imports/index.js";

export const badge = defineObject({
  apiName: "Badge",
  displayName: "Badge",
  pluralDisplayName: "Badges",
  primaryKeyPropertyApiName: "badgeId",
  titlePropertyApiName: "badgeId",
  properties: {
    badgeId: { type: "string" },
    employeeId: { type: "integer" },
  },
});

export const employeeBadges = defineLink({
  apiName: "employee-badges",
  one: { object: employee, metadata: { apiName: "badges" } },
  toMany: { object: badge, metadata: { apiName: "employee" } },
  manyForeignKeyProperty: "employeeId",
});
```

The generated modules are TypeScript files that import each other with `.js` extensions, so Node cannot load them as they are. Compile the output directory with `tsc` as an ES module project before you run maker, or publish it as a compiled package. The example above imports the compiled `./imports/index.js`.

> [!NOTE]
> An interface link constraint or an interface action type constraint cannot start from an imported interface. Define them only on interfaces in your own ontology.

## What is converted

| Metadata | Converted to | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shared property types | `SharedPropertyType` | API name, display name, description, and type. |
| Interfaces | `InterfaceType` | Properties, including interface-defined properties, links, and the interfaces they extend. Status is always active, and action type constraints are not included. |
| Object types | `ObjectType` | Properties, primary key, title, description, visibility, and shared property types. Status is active or experimental. `pluralDisplayName` is the display name with `s` added. |
| Action types | `ActionType` | Parameters only, with no logic rules. Status is active or experimental. |
| Link types | Not converted | Define links to imported object types yourself, as above. |

Marking properties are imported with the marking input name `not-applicable`, because the existing type already owns its marking configuration.

`maker-import` throws on types it cannot represent, naming the type:

- Property types other than the primitive, geospatial, media, attachment, marking, struct, array, vector, and geotime series types. A marking property must have a `markingType`.
- Struct fields that are arrays or structs, and struct main values that are arrays.
- Vector properties that support more than one search similarity function, or whose embedding model is missing settings.
- Vector action parameters, and action parameter types with no maker equivalent.

## Use it from code

The package also exports the conversion functions:

```ts title="scripts/import-ontology.ts"
import * as fs from "node:fs";

import type { OntologyFullMetadata } from "@osdk/foundry.ontologies";
import { convertOntologyFullMetadata, writeImportedOntology } from "@osdk/maker-import";

const metadata = JSON.parse(
  fs.readFileSync("ontology-full-metadata.json", "utf-8"),
) as OntologyFullMetadata;

const definition = convertOntologyFullMetadata(metadata);
console.log(Object.keys(definition.OBJECT_TYPE));

writeImportedOntology(metadata, ".ontology/imports");
```

| Function | Returns | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `convertOntologyFullMetadata(metadata)` | `OntologyDefinition` | Converts the metadata to maker's in-memory form, keyed by entity kind and API name, without writing files. |
| `writeImportedOntology(metadata, outputDir)` | `void` | Converts the metadata and writes the modules, as the CLI does. |

## Share types between ontology-as-code projects

To reuse types from another ontology-as-code project instead of from Foundry, compile that project with `maker --outputDir`. Maker writes the same module layout, plus `link-types` and `value-types` folders, and its `index.ts` records the package's namespace and version when it loads, so a consuming project can list it with `maker --dependencies <file>`. As with `maker-import` output, compile or publish the modules before you import them.

# Ontology as code

Source: https://older.zaini.me/osdk-ts/ontology-as-code

> Define object types, links, actions, and interfaces in TypeScript with @osdk/maker, compile them to Ontology IR, and develop against them locally.

Related Palantir Foundry documentation:
- [Ontology as code](https://www.palantir.com/docs/foundry/superrepo/core-concepts#ontology-as-code)

Ontology as code lets you define Ontology types in TypeScript files that live next to your app. `@osdk/maker` validates the definitions and compiles them into an Ontology intermediate representation (IR) file, and `@osdk/vite-plugin-oac` turns that IR into a generated SDK and a mock Foundry server for local development.

> [!WARNING]
> Every ontology-as-code package is pre-1.0 (`@osdk/maker` 0.82, `@osdk/vite-plugin-oac` 0.85, `@osdk/maker-import` 0.48) and treated as experimental. Definitions, CLI flags, and the IR format can change in any release. Pin exact versions and read the changelog before you upgrade.

## Packages

| Package | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `@osdk/maker` | The `define*` functions you write your ontology with, and the `maker` CLI that compiles it to IR. |
| `@osdk/vite-plugin-oac` | A Vite plugin that compiles the ontology on every change, generates an SDK from it, and serves a mock Foundry API from the dev server. See [Local development](https://older.zaini.me/osdk-ts/ontology-as-code/local-development.md). |
| `@osdk/maker-import` | Converts the metadata of an existing Foundry ontology into TypeScript files you can reference from your definitions. See [Import existing types](https://older.zaini.me/osdk-ts/ontology-as-code/import.md). |
| `@osdk/seed-helpers`, `@osdk/seed-compiler` | Build seed objects and links for the local Ontology server. See [Local development](https://older.zaini.me/osdk-ts/ontology-as-code/local-development.md#seed-data-for-the-local-ontology-server). |

## How it works

1. **Define.** You write object types, links, actions, interfaces, shared property types, and value types in `.ontology/ontology.mts`. Each `define*` call validates its input and registers the type.
2. **Compile.** The `maker` CLI imports that file and writes the IR to `ontology.json`, plus `value-types.json` when you define value types.
3. **Develop locally.** In a Vite app, `@osdk/vite-plugin-oac` runs `maker` on every change, converts the IR to Ontology metadata, generates an SDK into `.osdk/src`, and answers OSDK requests from the dev server with seeded data.
4. **Ship.** The IR file is the artifact. None of these packages uploads or installs it into a Foundry stack.

## Install

```npm
npm install --save-dev @osdk/maker
```

`@osdk/maker` installs a `maker` binary. For local development, also install the Vite plugin; see [Local development](https://older.zaini.me/osdk-ts/ontology-as-code/local-development.md#install).

The CLI loads your ontology file with Node's own `import()`, so a `.mts` or `.ts` entry file needs a Node.js version that strips TypeScript types natively: 22.18 or later, or 23.6 or later. On older versions, write the file as `.mjs`.

## Project layout

```text
.ontology/
  ontology.mts
  seed.ts
  ontology-schema-lock.json
.osdk/
  src/
src/
package.json
vite.config.ts
```

| Path | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `.ontology/ontology.mts` | Your definitions. The Vite plugin reads exactly this file name. |
| `.ontology/seed.ts` | Mock data for the Vite plugin's local server. |
| `.ontology/ontology-schema-lock.json` | Written by `maker --write-locks` once an interface opts into [schema migrations](https://older.zaini.me/osdk-ts/ontology-as-code/interfaces.md#schema-migrations). Commit it. |
| `.osdk/src` | The SDK the Vite plugin generates. Do not edit it by hand. |

## Write an ontology

The ontology file is a module whose top-level `define*` calls register types as they run. Export each result so other files, such as a seed file or another ontology, can import it.

This file defines the `Employee` and `Office` object types, the links between them, a `Worker` interface, and a `modifyEmployee` action:

```ts title=".ontology/ontology.mts"
import {
  defineInterface,
  defineLink,
  defineModifyObjectAction,
  defineObject,
  defineSharedPropertyType,
} from "@osdk/maker";

export const name = defineSharedPropertyType({
  apiName: "name",
  type: "string",
  displayName: "Name",
});

export const worker = defineInterface({
  apiName: "Worker",
  displayName: "Worker",
  properties: { name },
});

export const office = defineObject({
  apiName: "Office",
  displayName: "Office",
  pluralDisplayName: "Offices",
  primaryKeyPropertyApiName: "officeId",
  titlePropertyApiName: "name",
  properties: {
    officeId: { type: "string", displayName: "Office ID" },
    name: { type: "string" },
    city: { type: "string" },
  },
});

export const employee = defineObject({
  apiName: "Employee",
  displayName: "Employee",
  pluralDisplayName: "Employees",
  primaryKeyPropertyApiName: "employeeId",
  titlePropertyApiName: "fullName",
  properties: {
    employeeId: { type: "integer", displayName: "Employee ID" },
    fullName: { type: "string", displayName: "Full name" },
    jobTitle: { type: "string" },
    department: { type: "string" },
    startDate: { type: "date" },
    salary: { type: "double" },
    skills: { type: "string", array: true },
    leadId: { type: "integer" },
    officeId: { type: "string" },
  },
  implementsInterfaces: [
    {
      implements: worker,
      propertyMapping: [{ interfaceProperty: "name", mapsTo: "fullName" }],
    },
  ],
});

export const officeOccupants = defineLink({
  apiName: "office-occupants",
  one: { object: office, metadata: { apiName: "occupants" } },
  toMany: { object: employee, metadata: { apiName: "office" } },
  manyForeignKeyProperty: "officeId",
});

export const employeeReports = defineLink({
  apiName: "employee-reports",
  one: { object: employee, metadata: { apiName: "reports" } },
  toMany: { object: employee, metadata: { apiName: "lead" } },
  manyForeignKeyProperty: "leadId",
});

export const modifyEmployee = defineModifyObjectAction({
  apiName: "modify-employee",
  objectType: employee,
});
```

In the SDK generated from this file, `Employee` has the links `office` and `lead` (one object each) and `reports` (many), `Office` has `occupants`, and the action is `modifyEmployee`: action API names must be lowercase and hyphenated, and the SDK generator converts them to camelCase. The `leadId` and `officeId` properties are the foreign keys the links join on.

Compile it:

```sh
npx maker -i .ontology/ontology.mts -o ontology.json
```

Each `define*` function throws when its input is invalid, for example when a title or primary key property is missing, an API name breaks the naming rules, or two types share an API name. `maker` reports the first error and exits with code 1; run it with `-v` to print the stack trace.

## API names and namespaces

`--apiNamespace com.example` prefixes the API names of the object types, interfaces, shared property types, and action types you define, so `Employee` becomes `com.example.Employee`. Pass names without the prefix in your definitions. Link type API names are not prefixed, and value types are prefixed only when you set `namespacePrefix: true`.

| Name | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Object type | Starts with a letter, then letters and digits, with optional `.`-separated segments, at most 100 characters. |
| Property, link side | Starts with a letter, then letters, digits, and `_`, at most 100 characters. |
| Action type | Lowercase letters and digits, in segments separated by `-` or `.`. |
| Link type | Converted to a lowercase, hyphenated ID (`officeOccupants` and `office_occupants` both become `office-occupants`), which must start with a letter. |
| All | Cannot be a reserved word: `ontology`, `object`, `property`, `link`, `relation`, `rid`, `primaryKey`, `typeId`, or `ontologyObject`, in any case. |

## `maker` CLI

```sh
maker [options]
```

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-i`, `--input` | `string` | `.ontology/ontology.ts` | The ontology file to load. |
| `-o`, `--output` | `string` | `ontology.json` | Where to write the IR. |
| `--valueTypesOutput` | `string` | `value-types.json` | Where to write value types. Written only when the ontology defines or imports value types. |
| `--apiNamespace` | `string` | `""` | Prefix for API names, such as `com.example`. A trailing `.` is added for you. Must match `^[a-z0-9-]+(\.[a-z0-9-]+)*\.$`. |
| `-d`, `--outputDir` | `string` | | Also write each defined type as a TypeScript module under `<dir>/codegen`, with an `index.ts` that re-exports them. Other ontologies can import this output; see [Import existing types](https://older.zaini.me/osdk-ts/ontology-as-code/import.md#share-types-between-ontology-as-code-projects). |
| `--dependencies` | `string` | | Write the namespaces and versions of imported ontology packages to this JSON file. |
| `--generateCodeSnippets` | `boolean` | `false` | Write OSDK usage snippets for each object type, action type, and interface. |
| `--codeSnippetPackageName` | `string` | `""` | The SDK package name shown in the snippets. |
| `--codeSnippetDir` | `string` | `./` | Where to write the snippets. |
| `--randomnessKey` | `string` | | A UUID recorded in the IR to keep generated entities unique. Rejected if it is not a UUID. |
| `--lockfile` | `string` | `ontology-schema-lock.json` next to the input | The interface schema lockfile. |
| `--writeLocks` | `boolean` | | Update the lockfile instead of failing when it is out of date. |
| `-y`, `--yes` | `boolean` | | Accept detected schema migration finalizations and deletions without a prompt. Requires `--writeLocks`. |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | `count` | | `-v` logs debug output and stack traces; `-vv` logs trace output. |
